blocks.content: Both volcanoes and earthquakes are direct surface manifestations of the dynamic endogenetic forces driven by plate tectonics.

rows: Extrusive eruption of molten magma, ash, and volcanic gases
Sudden release of stored kinetic strain energy as seismic waves
Buoyancy and gas expansion driving magma upward
Tectonic faulting and fracture of rigid rock strata
Shallow (0-70 km), Intermediate (70-300 km), and Deep (300-700 km)

items: Deep-focus earthquakes (Benioff zones) occur strictly at convergent/subduction boundaries, not at divergent boundaries.
Harmonic tremors (continuous rhythmic seismic signals) indicate active magma movement and serve as a key precursor to volcanic eruptions.
The Mid-Continental Belt experiences major earthquakes (e.g., the Himalayan region) but lacks active volcanism because continental crust-to-crust collision lacks oceanic crust subduction.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Volcanoes and earthquakes both primarily occur along active tectonic plate boundaries, particularly subduction zones and divergent ridges.
The Pacific 'Ring of Fire' hosts over 75% of the world's active volcanoes and approximately 80% of the world's largest earthquakes.
Volcanic earthquakes are generated by the movement of magma beneath the surface, producing distinctive harmonic tremors.
Subduction zones (convergent boundaries) feature deep-focus earthquakes and explosive composite volcanoes.
Mid-oceanic ridges (divergent boundaries) feature shallow-focus earthquakes and quiet basaltic volcanism.
